notes.meaning: Mark records that the soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross at the third hour, which was about nine o'clock in the morning by Jewish reckoning. This was the exact time when priests offered the regular morning sacrifice at the temple in Jerusalem. While the religious leaders should have been leading public worship, they were busy putting Jesus to death.

The Roman soldiers put a written sign above Jesus' head listing His charge as "The King of the Jews." Pilate wrote this title to mock both Jesus and the Jewish leaders who demanded His death. Yet God turned their mockery into a public statement of the truth, declaring that Jesus truly is the King of His people.

Two robbers were crucified on either side of Jesus, placing Him in the middle as if He were the worst criminal of the group. His enemies intended this arrangement to cause Him deep shame and disgrace. Even in death, Jesus stood right in the middle of lawbreakers so He could save sinners.

This verse recalls the prophecy of Isaiah, showing that the Messiah would be counted among lawbreakers. Although Jesus was entirely innocent and holy, He allowed Himself to be treated as a criminal. In this way, He took the penalty that guilty people deserved upon Himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that this verse is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, meaning early copyists likely brought it in from Luke 22:37.

notes.meaning: People walking along the road shook their heads and hurled cruel insults at Jesus. They brought up His earlier words about the temple and dared Him to prove His power by climbing down from the cross to save Himself. Without knowing it, their mocking words and head-shaking fulfilled what the Psalms had long predicted about the Messiah's suffering.

The chief priests and teachers of the law ridiculed Jesus among themselves, pointing out that He had healed and saved others but could not rescue Himself. They claimed they would believe in Him as the King of Israel if He would only perform the miracle of coming down from the cross. Even the criminals crucified alongside Him joined in mocking Him at first.

A thick, supernatural darkness spread over the whole land from noon until three o'clock in the afternoon. Because Passover took place during a full moon, this darkness could not have been a natural solar eclipse. It stood as a sign of God's heavy judgment against sin and the dark sorrow Jesus endured for our sake.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the darkness as a literary picture borrowed from Old Testament prophecy or ancient mourning traditions rather than a literal historical event.

notes.meaning: At three in the afternoon, Jesus cried out in Aramaic, asking God why He had forsaken Him. He used the opening words of Psalm 22 to voice the deep agony in His soul. At that moment, as Jesus took on the burden of human sin, He experienced the painful withdrawal of His Father's comforting favor.

Some people standing nearby misheard Jesus' cry of "Eloi" and thought He was asking the prophet Elijah to rescue Him. One person soaked a sponge in sour wine, held it up on a stick to moisten His lips, and told the crowd to wait and see if Elijah would really show up. Their remarks were one last cruel attempt to mock Jesus in His dying moments.

Jesus let out one last loud cry and breathed His final breath. Dying victims of crucifixion were normally too weak to speak, so this strong shout showed that His life was not merely slipping away by accident. He had the strength of will to willingly lay down His life into the Father's hands.

At the moment Jesus died, the thick curtain inside the temple ripped in two from the top all the way to the bottom. Since it tore from the very top, it showed that God Himself had torn it open. This event proved that the old temple system was ending and that Jesus had opened a direct path for all people into God's holy presence.

The Roman army officer supervising the execution watched Jesus cry out and take His last breath. Seeing how differently Jesus died compared to other men, the soldier confessed that this man was truly the Son of God. A pagan soldier, who knew nothing of the Jewish scriptures, became the first person at the cross to recognize Jesus' true glory.

Several faithful women watched these painful events from a safe distance, including Mary Magdalene, Salome, and Mary the mother of James and Joses. These women had traveled with Jesus in Galilee, providing food and care for Him and His followers. When most of the male disciples had scattered in fear, these devoted women stayed near to the very end.

Late afternoon arrived on Friday, known as the Preparation Day before the Sabbath. Jewish law stated that executed bodies could not remain hanging on a wood cross overnight, and the Sabbath was due to start at sunset. The short amount of time remaining meant someone had to act quickly to take Jesus down and bury Him properly.

Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy, respected member of the Jewish high court who had been quietly looking forward to God's kingdom. Though he had previously kept his faith in Jesus quiet, he boldly went to Governor Pilate to request the Lord's body. He risked his social standing and safety to ensure Jesus received a decent burial.

Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was dead so soon, because people hung on crosses often lasted for several days. He called the centurion to ask for an official report to be completely sure of the death. Once the officer verified that Jesus had truly passed away, Pilate gave Joseph permission to take the corpse.

Joseph bought an expensive linen cloth, gently took Jesus' body down from the cross, and wrapped Him in it. He placed the body into his own new tomb that was carved out of solid rock, then rolled a heavy circular stone across the entrance to protect it. By being buried in a rich man's private tomb, Jesus fulfilled the prophecy that He would be with the rich in His death.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses sat nearby and carefully watched where Joseph placed Jesus' body. They noted the exact location so they could easily find it when they returned after the Sabbath to complete the anointing with spices. Their close attention provided dependable eyewitness proof that Jesus was truly placed in that specific tomb.
